page_placements.theme: Data spectra, target structure and feature learning explain conditional scaling regimes

record.tranche_reason: The study derives and evaluates data-size learning curves using a countable-feature memorization model, a different method and system from language-model scaling studies. Its results bear on whether power-law learning curves and extrapolation hold, but it does not test language models directly.
record.gate_note: The study focuses on sample size in a toy classification model; it does not sweep language-model parameters, training tokens, or compute, or test a compute-optimal allocation. Its own theoretical and experimental results on learning-curve shape are included. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyses a toy memorization classifier on countable features, not a language model or any neural network. Its learning curves are for 0-1 error against sample size and come from that classifier. No version names this kind of system, and the author warns there is 'no indication that our findings transfer'. Its results offer a theoretical account of data-size power laws but do not test any version. They are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author concludes that the simplest toy model yields power laws for many but not all data distributions, with β=α/(1+α) for Zipf data. He does not know whether that relation has wider validity. He says a single run suffices for time-averaged error. He calls the model totally unrealistic for deep learning, yet believes it captures a true reason for data scaling laws. He says transfer to neural networks, model size or compute is beyond scope.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a countable-feature memorization classifier with deterministic labels and 0-1 error, and focuses on data size. It does not train language models or measure parameter-count or compute scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: The learning-curve form and exponent vary with the feature-probability distribution; the fitted exponent for the word-frequency curve varies with the fitting range.

fits_no_version.finding: In a countable-feature memorizing classifier, Zipf-distributed features with θi∝i^-(α+1) give error ≈cα n^-β with β=α/(1+α). Fitted exponents match theory (0.500 for α=1, 0.091 for α=0.1). Exponentially distributed features give a 1/n power law; finite uniform support gives exponential decay of the instantaneous error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In simple memorization models, the data-size learning-curve exponent is set by the feature-frequency distribution, and power laws are not universal.

fits_no_version.finding: For real word frequencies (Calgary book1), the learning curve is roughly a power law for moderate n. It decays faster than the extrapolated power-law fit for large n, because the support is finite, and the fitted exponent depends on the fit range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning curves built from empirical finite-support data bend away from a single power law at large n in memorization models.

record.problems: The model is explicitly a toy memorization model rather than a neural language model. The empirical word-frequency example uses one text file and its learning curve departs from a single power law at large sample sizes. The paper itself says transfer to neural networks is unknown.

untested.parts: All of it: no language-model pretraining loss, and no scaling in parameters or compute.
All of it: no extrapolation from small to large LM runs (only a toy fit-range extrapolation).
All of it: no neural models in other modalities or training regimes.
All of it for real models: no comparison of fitting choices across trained models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's labels are dropped because the rows measure a non-neural toy classifier, not the systems the versions name. The reader's V2 'challenges' rested on a toy fit-range extrapolation, not on LM runs. Row r6 mis-transcribes the full-range fit (see row_fixes). The time-averaged error and variance results (Section 4) and the noisy-label analysis (Appendix C) are unrecorded, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss; scaling with parameter count or compute; behavior when other factors are not bottlenecks.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to language-model runs orders of magnitude larger.
Whether compute-optimal parameter and token allocations depend on setup or fitting choices; disagreements between published allocation laws.

rows.subject: Algorithm A
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed and experimentally plotted expected error against sample size for a finite uniform feature distribution.
rows.measure: Expected instantaneous 0-1 error as a function of sample size
rows.value: For m equally likely features, EEn=(1−1/m)^n≈e^(−n/m); the m=10 experiment shows this exponential decay.
rows.note: This finite-support toy setting is an explicit case where the instantaneous error is exponential rather than a power law.
rows.check: Toy memorization classifier, not a language or neural model, so it bears on no version. The instantaneous error decays exponentially here. The paper notes the time-averaged error decays as 1/N, which the row omits.

relation.reason: The paper discusses deep-learning scaling laws and proposes a possible explanatory mechanism through a toy model, without testing those laws in the systems named by the claim versions.

tranche.reason: The results concern a tabular memorization classifier's error against sample size. They do not test a listed version for language models or deep-learning training regimes; transfer to neural networks is explicitly unresolved.

source_check.notes: Row states describe the toy classifier's curves only; they do not establish verdicts on any listed version. Figure 2 fits expected curves, and r4 is an analytic result.

statements.correction: Countable-feature memorizing classifier; Zipf frequencies proportional to i^−(1+α); theoretical β=α/(1+α); α=1: theoretical β=0.500, fitted β=0.501; α=0.1: theoretical and fitted β≈0.091.
statements.problem: The classifier and theoretical relationship are correct, but 0.500 is the theoretical exponent for α=1; the fitted instantaneous-error exponent is 0.501.
